messages.author: b74d47d59ad17fb5
messages.subject: Temp file cleanup
parts:
I think rmr should clean up the tmp files it creates in the local file system. 

If I understand correctly, there are global, local, map, combine and reduce environments created, saved and disseminated across the cluster for each mapreduce call. 
As far as I could see, they are not reused after the initial call. So it would make sense (and would be considered good practice) for rmr to clean up after itself when the run is complete. 

Am I missing anything?

Thanks!
-Saar

P.S. great job on the new release!

messages.author: 6ac7e7dfbe4f6c38
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1327] Temp file cleanup
parts:
Hi Saar,
rmr uses exclusively temporary files as returned by tempfile(). Since those are cleared at the end of the session, it was never considered paramount to add additional logic to have them deleted earlier, but since some environment files can be big, maybe it wouldn't be such a bad idea to look into it. I notice nonetheless copy of those files accumulating when I am using standalone mode in Hadoop. My guess is that it is a Hadoop bug, but I never bothered reporting it so I am  not sure. In theory a running job is assigned a working directory that starts clean and is removed at the end (it's a feature called distributed cache). All the files rmr distributed to HDFS should be in that directory. This clearly is not happening at least in some instances. Therefore I would suggest that you open an issue on the rmr issue tracker, provide some example names for those files and their complete path and also I would like to know in which mode you are running hadoop. This is harder to fix than it seems since tasks may share some of those files, so I am not sure I can just delete them after reading them. The master R instance doesn't know where they are, the location being under Hadoop controls, and I am not sure I have API access to that piece of information. Anyway thanks for the report and we'll try to get to the bottom of it.


Antonio

messages.author: 63023c771a070260
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1327] Temp file cleanup
parts:
From Hadoop's definitive guide

The tasktracker also maintains a reference count for the number of 
tasks using each file in the cache. Before the task has run, the 
file’s reference count is incremented by one; then after the task has 
run, the count is decreased by one. Only when the count reaches zero 
it is eligible for deletion, since no tasks are using it. Files are 
deleted to make room for a new file when the cache exceeds a certain 
size—10 GB by default. The cache size may be changed by setting the 
configuration property local.cache.size, which is measured in bytes. 


Antonio

messages.author: b74d47d59ad17fb5
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1327] Temp file cleanup
parts:
I'm not sure we're talking about the same files, so I'll make sure before I go ahead and create an issue in the tracker: I was referring to the files created locally (map.file, reduce.file, combine.file, rmr.local.env, and rmr.global.env). When I run a long sequences of iterative mapreduce jobs (k-means iterations, for example) with different parameter values (number of clusters, starting values, dataset generating parameters) I get an accumulation of files in the local file system, under the current sessions' temporary directory. True, it should be cleaned up when the session ends, but It's been more than once that I've run out of space during long sessions... 

I know I can address it by assigning ample space for these temp files and directing there using TMPDIR, TEMP or TMP, but I think (and I've been told by my cluster admin) that it would be good form for my own application to clean up after itself. These file names are available inside rmr.stream(), but are not accessible from outside that function (I think). It would be nice to have them deleted after the try.catch(system(...)) call. 

(I'm using a 12 node Hortonworks hadoop cluster, not a standalone setup, but I think this is not what we're talking about. If the cluster configuration actually matters, I'd gladly post the relevant settings)

-Saar
